title: Needle-felted weasel
subtitle: A slender chestnut-and-cream stoat-family figure in merino
excerpt: Felt a compact weasel in warm chestnut merino with a white underside, about 10 cm nose to tail. The long, low body is the challenge; a rolled core keeps the shape from thickening mid-spine.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional needle-felting guild practice. Mustelid forms are a standard British needle-felting subject; the elongated low-slung body requires the compact-core approach described here.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to tangle wool fibres together without water or heat. Each stab compresses and locks the fibres.
Wool fibre drawn out into a continuous ribbon, the standard input for needle-felting projects.

content.text: is a long, narrow body in chestnut brown with a straight cream-white underside running from chin to belly. The finished piece is about 10 cm nose to tail and sits naturally in a slight S-curve. Build the body from a tight, firm core rolled from chestnut
before adding the legs and head, or the spine will thicken unevenly as you needle.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. Keep the finger guard on the supporting hand throughout.

items.name: Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Roll a generous length of chestnut roving into a tight sausage about 12 cm long. Needle felt on all sides, turning the piece frequently, until the core is firm and about 9 cm long. Keep the ends slightly tapered: the neck end thinner, the hindquarters slightly broader. A firm core is important for this breed shape because the weasel is long relative to its girth; a loose core spreads and looks more like a rabbit than a mustelid.

Pull a thin layer of cream roving and needle it in a straight strip along the belly, from the chin to the base of the tail. Work the edges inward so the colour change is a clean, straight line along each flank. Weasels have a sharp demarcation between dorsal chestnut and ventral white; blending at the edges gives a stoat look rather than a weasel.

Roll a small ball of chestnut roving for the head, about 2 cm in diameter when firm. Needle it to a slightly flattened oval, then attach it to the neck end of the body by pressing the head against the body and needling repeatedly through the join, rotating the piece to lock the join from all angles. Build a small muzzle by needling a little extra roving onto the front of the head and shaping it into a blunt point.

Roll four short sausages of chestnut roving for the legs, each about 2 cm long when firm. Needle each one until firm, then attach two at the shoulder and two at the hindquarters. The legs are short and do not need posed; needle them flat against the body so the weasel sits rather than stands. Roll a thin taper of chestnut roving for the tail, about 2.5 cm long, and needle it to the back end of the body.

Needle a small cream or white patch around the muzzle to lighten the face slightly. Stitch the black seed bead eyes in position just above the midline of the head using strong thread, pulling firmly so the beads sit close to the surface. Needle a tiny indent at each nostril. Trim loose surface fibres with small scissors.

items.problem: The body is too round and barrel-shaped
items.cause: The core was needled from the sides only, building up the girth rather than compressing it lengthways
items.fix: Press the core firmly between your fingers to establish the length, then needle from the ends inward to keep the length-to-girth ratio right from the start.

items.problem: The cream belly edge looks blurry and blended
items.cause: Too much roving was applied at the flank edge, or the edge fibres were needled diagonally rather than straight inward
items.fix: Remove loose surface fibres and re-needle the edge with the needle angled sharply inward along the flank line.
